title: Ram, Allah, and Many Names
hook: a guru gives Kabir one name, Ram, and Kabir sings it beside Allah
carry: truth is one; the wise call it many names
tomorrow: if God's not in the temple or the mosque, then where?

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti asks whom you love, not your birth, and Kabir's flowers went half to each side. Today, the names he used for God.

Before dawn in Benares, a young weaver lies down on the steps of the river ghat, in the dark. A great teacher, Ramananda, comes down to bathe, steps on him, and cries out: Ram! The legend says Kabir took that one word as his guru's gift, and you met that story back in year three. One word, from a guru: Ram. Here's what Kabir did with it. In his songs, Ram isn't only the prince of Ayodhya. And the name sits beside others: Hari, Allah, Karim. Same song, same breath. A muddle? Or a teaching?
screen: `A FOOT IN THE DARK: RAM!` → `ONE WORD FROM A GURU.` → `RAM, HARI, ALLAH, KARIM.`

segments.voice: Here's one song, in paraphrase, from the English version Tagore made. Hari is in the east, Allah is in the west. Look in your heart, and there you'll find both Karim and Ram. It ends: he is my guru, he is my pir. Guru is the Hindu word for a spiritual teacher; pir is the Sufi one. Hindus have an old line that explains why this sounds like home to Hindu ears. The Rig Veda says, in paraphrase: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Ekam sat. That's why Hindu prayer is full of names. Families chant the thousand names of Vishnu, and repeating the Name, japa, is itself worship. For Kabir, Ram was that one truth, beyond any form, and the Name was the whole path. Islam honors many names too: the most beautiful names of God, Karim the Generous and Rahim the Merciful among them, all names of the one God, with no image. That's an honest difference: Hindu names often come with forms and stories. A couplet credited to Kabir, in paraphrase: the Hindu says Ram is dear to me, the Turk, meaning the Muslim, says Rahman, the Merciful; the two fought and died, and neither knew the secret. So Kabir didn't coin a third word that swallowed both. He kept each name whole, in its own tongue.
screen: `HARI EAST, ALLAH WEST. MY GURU, MY PIR.` · `EKAM SAT: TRUTH IS ONE.` · `ISLAM'S BEAUTIFUL NAMES.` · then, large: `EACH NAME KEPT WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Japa is one of the oldest Hindu practices: repeating a name of God. If you pray, choose the name you grew up with, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, and say it slowly, eleven times, on your fingers or a mala. Let each one land before the next. If you don't pray, use a word that means peace to you. Then, for one breath, hold in mind someone who calls the holy by a different name, and wish them well.
Hindu-Muslim shared saints. Here, a poet who called God by names from both homes, side by side.
Keep this: truth is one, and the wise call it by many names. Kabir kept each one whole. That's today.

howItsDone: Hindus chant many names of God, from japa on a mala to the thousand names of Vishnu, and often quote the Rig Veda's line that truth is one and the wise call it by many names; Kabir's songs, with Ram and Hari beside Allah and Karim, are sung in Hindu devotional settings.
